title: ASP.NET Core
html:
ASP.NET Core

The pipeline

A request passes through ordered middleware, each able to act before and after the next. Order is behaviour, not style: authentication must precede authorisation, exception handling must be outermost to catch anything after it, and static files placed early avoid the rest of the pipeline entirely.

A middleware that does not call the next one short-circuits, which is how caching and authorisation failures return without doing the work.

Dependency injection and lifetimes

Three lifetimes, and choosing wrong is the most common structural bug:

  • Transient - a new instance per request for it. Safe, occasionally wasteful.
  • Scoped - one per HTTP request. The right default for anything holding request state, including a database context.
  • Singleton - one for the application. Must be thread-safe.

The trap is a captive dependency: a singleton holding a scoped service. The scoped object is captured on first use and then lives forever, shared across requests. A database context captured that way accumulates tracked entities and leaks across users. The framework's scope validation catches this in development - leave it on.

Configuration and secrets

Layered, later sources winning: appsettings, environment-specific appsettings, environment variables, command line. That layering is what lets a deployment override a file without editing it.

Secrets do not belong in appsettings, because appsettings belongs in source control. Environment variables for simple cases, a managed secret store beyond that. The double underscore in Section__Key maps to nested configuration.

Async all the way

Use async for I/O so the thread is returned to the pool while waiting. Two rules that matter more than they look:

  • Never block on async - no .Result, no .Wait(). Under load it exhausts the thread pool and deadlocks in some contexts, and the symptom is a hang with no error.
  • Accept a cancellation token on every async entry point and pass it down. When a client disconnects, the work should stop, not run to completion for nobody.

Returning errors

Consistency matters more than the specific shape. ProblemDetails is the standard: a machine-readable body with a status, a title and a detail. Validation failures return 400 with the field errors; not found is 404; unauthenticated is 401 and unauthorised-but-known is 403 - those two are distinct and conflating them confuses every client.

Never let an exception message reach a client. It leaks paths, queries and versions.

Model binding and validation

Bound from the route, query, body and headers. Validate at the boundary and trust the interior - a request object validated once should not be re-checked in three layers.

Bind to a purpose-built request type rather than to a domain entity. Binding straight to an entity is over-posting: a field the caller was never meant to set arrives anyway.

Common mistakes

  • Middleware in the wrong order, most often authorisation before authentication.
  • A scoped service captured by a singleton.
  • Blocking on async and calling the resulting hang a performance problem.
  • Returning entities directly, coupling the API shape to the database shape.
  • Ignoring the cancellation token, so a cancelled request keeps working.
